title: The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis (1952)
text:
Citation
Turing, A. M. (1952). The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological Sciences, 237(641), 37–72. https://doi.org/10.1098/rstb.1952.0012
Read the paper.

title: The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis (1952)
text:
Overview
Turing proposes that biological patterns can emerge from a system of interacting chemical substances, which he calls morphogens. These substances react with one another and diffuse through tissue.
A spatially uniform state can become unstable under the right conditions. Small differences in morphogen concentration may then grow rather than disappear, producing nonuniform patterns.

title: The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis (1952)
text:
Main Ideas

Morphogens

Morphogens are chemical substances involved in the development of biological form.
Cells do not follow a fixed developmental blueprint.
Instead, cells respond to local morphogen concentrations that change over time.



Reaction and Diffusion
The model combines two processes:

local chemical reactions;
diffusion across space.

A simplified reaction–diffusion system is
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}
=
D_u \nabla^2 u + f(u,v),
\]
\[
\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}
=
D_v \nabla^2 v + g(u,v).
\]
where

\(u\) and \(v\) are morphogen concentrations.
\(D_u\) and \(D_v\) are diffusion coefficients.
\(f(u,v)\) and \(g(u,v)\) describe the local reaction terms.
\(\nabla^2\) is the Laplacian operator.



Diffusion-Driven Instability

A spatially uniform equilibrium can become unstable when diffusion is added.
Diffusion normally smooths differences in concentration.
In a coupled reaction–diffusion system, unequal diffusion rates can instead amplify small perturbations.
Those perturbations can develop into stable spatial patterns.



Pattern Formation
Possible outcomes include

spots;
stripes;
waves;
repeated structures;
other spatial arrangements.

The resulting pattern depends on

the reaction terms;
the diffusion coefficients;
the geometry of the domain;
the initial perturbations.

title: The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis (1952)
text:
Questions

Why does diffusion stabilize some systems but destabilize others?
What determines whether spots or stripes emerge?
How does the geometry of the domain influence the final pattern?
How should a reaction–diffusion model be adapted to an irregular butterfly wing?
Can diffusion on a graph preserve meaningful geometric information?
Which aspects of butterfly wing development are well described by Turing models, and which require additional biological mechanisms?

title: The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis (1952)
text:
Connections to My Research
This paper provides the mathematical foundation for my butterfly wing project.
I’m interested in

representing wing structure as a graph;
modeling morphogen diffusion across that graph;
comparing simulated patterns with real butterfly wings.

A graph-based analogue replaces the continuous Laplacian with a graph Laplacian.
A simplified system becomes
\[
\frac{d\mathbf{u}}{dt}
=
-D_uL\mathbf{u}
+
\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}),
\]
\[
\frac{d\mathbf{v}}{dt}
=
-D_vL\mathbf{v}
+
\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}),
\]
where

(L) is the graph Laplacian;
() and () are morphogen concentrations defined on the graph.

title: The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis (1952)
text:
Notes

Homogeneous Equilibrium

Morphogen concentrations are constant throughout the domain.
Concentrations do not change over time.
The reaction system must be stable before diffusion is introduced.
Turing instability occurs when diffusion destabilizes this equilibrium.



Linear Stability

Small perturbations are analyzed by linearizing the reaction terms near an equilibrium.
The Jacobian matrix is

\[
J =
\begin{pmatrix}
f_u & f_v \\
g_u & g_v
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The entries of (J) determine the local stability of the reaction system.
With diffusion, each spatial mode evolves independently.
Some modes decay while others grow into observable patterns.



Geometry

Geometry determines which spatial modes are possible.
Boundary conditions influence how morphogens behave near the edges of the domain.
Domain shape affects the resulting biological pattern.
Geometry is therefore a central component of models for butterfly wings, shells, and animal coat markings.

title: The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis (1952)
text:
Vocabulary

Morphogen — A chemical signaling molecule whose concentration varies across tissue and provides positional information during development.
Homogeneous equilibrium — A steady state in which morphogen concentrations are the same everywhere in space and remain constant over time.
Perturbation — A small disturbance from an equilibrium state used to test whether the system returns to equilibrium or evolves into a new pattern.
Linear stability — A method of analyzing how small perturbations behave near an equilibrium by approximating the system with its linear terms.
Diffusion coefficient — A parameter that determines how quickly a morphogen spreads through space.
Laplacian — A differential operator, denoted (^2), that measures how a quantity diffuses by comparing its value to the surrounding region.
Eigenmode — A spatial pattern of variation that grows or decays independently during stability analysis. The dominant growing eigenmode determines the emerging biological pattern.
Boundary condition — A mathematical constraint imposed at the edges of the domain that influences how diffusion and reactions behave.
Diffusion-driven instability (Turing instability) — A phenomenon in which diffusion, rather than smoothing differences, destabilizes an otherwise stable homogeneous equilibrium and produces spatial patterns.
Graph Laplacian — The graph-theoretic analogue of the continuous Laplacian. It models diffusion on discrete structures such as networks or graph representations of butterfly wings.

Read the paper.

title: On Pattern Formation Mechanisms for Lepidopteran Wing Patterns and Mammalian Coat Markings (1981)
text:
Why I’m Reading It
This paper is especially relevant to my butterfly wing project because it is one of the earliest mathematical attempts to explain wing pattern formation through diffusion and gene activation rather than simply describing the observed patterns.
It also serves as an important bridge between Turing’s abstract reaction–diffusion theory and biologically motivated models of butterfly development.

title: On Pattern Formation Mechanisms for Lepidopteran Wing Patterns and Mammalian Coat Markings (1981)
text:
Overview
Murray proposes a mathematical mechanism capable of generating common butterfly wing patterns using a diffusing morphogen coupled with a threshold gene-activation process. He then compares the predictions of the model with experimental results from butterfly and moth wings.
The second half of the paper extends similar mathematical ideas to mammalian coat patterns, arguing that geometry and scale may explain much of the diversity observed in nature.

title: On Pattern Formation Mechanisms for Lepidopteran Wing Patterns and Mammalian Coat Markings (1981)
text:
Main Ideas

Pattern Formation Requires a Mechanism

The goal is to explain how biological patterns arise, not simply describe them.
Mathematical models should propose mechanisms that can generate observed patterns.
The focus is on developmental processes rather than static pigmentation.



Diffusing Morphogens

A morphogen is released from localized sources on the developing wing.
Diffusion produces a spatial concentration gradient.
Cells measure the local morphogen concentration.
Developmental responses depend on concentration thresholds.
Temporary chemical gradients produce lasting spatial patterns.



Gene Activation as a Switch

Morphogen concentration does not continuously determine pigment.
Cells permanently switch developmental states once a critical threshold is exceeded.
The developmental decision persists even after the morphogen disappears.
Threshold activation stabilizes the final wing pattern.



Geometry Matters

Wing geometry is an active component of pattern formation.
Changing wing size can alter the resulting pattern.
Changing wing shape changes morphogen distributions.
Vein arrangement influences diffusion pathways.
The same governing equations can generate different patterns solely because of geometry.

title: On Pattern Formation Mechanisms for Lepidopteran Wing Patterns and Mammalian Coat Markings (1981)

Figures 4–8

Illustrate how changes in geometry and parameters influence the resulting patterns.

title: On Pattern Formation Mechanisms for Lepidopteran Wing Patterns and Mammalian Coat Markings (1981)
text:
Questions

Can Murray’s continuous diffusion model can be reformulated on a graph using graph Laplacians?
How well has this model held up over the last forty years?
Which parts of the mechanism have experimental support today?
How would the model change if diffusion occurred on a graph instead of a continuous surface?
Could real wing vein networks be extracted automatically from photographs and used directly in simulations?
How do modern models incorporate gene regulatory networks in addition to morphogen diffusion?

title: On Pattern Formation Mechanisms for Lepidopteran Wing Patterns and Mammalian Coat Markings (1981)
text:
Vocabulary

Morphogen — A signaling molecule whose concentration varies across space and provides positional cues to developing cells.
Reaction–diffusion — A mathematical model in which interacting chemicals react locally while diffusing through tissue, producing spatial patterns.
Determination stream — A moving developmental boundary that records where morphogen concentration first exceeds the activation threshold, leaving behind permanently determined cells.
Positional information — Information encoded by a cell’s location, often inferred from local morphogen concentration, that guides developmental fate.
Threshold activation — The process by which a developmental response occurs only when morphogen concentration exceeds a critical value.
Gene switch — A regulatory mechanism in which cells permanently change developmental state once a threshold is crossed.
Diffusion field — The spatial distribution of morphogen concentration over the developing wing at a given time.
Geometry — The shape, size, and internal structure of the wing that influence how morphogens spread.
Scale — The physical dimensions of the tissue, which affect diffusion distances and therefore the resulting pattern.
Boundary conditions — Mathematical constraints imposed at the edges of the wing that determine how morphogens behave at tissue boundaries.

title: Collaboration Networks
text:
I am developing an agent-based model of evolving collaboration networks with nonlinear preferential attachment.
The model examines how attachment bias affects network growth, degree inequality, and concentration around highly connected individuals.

title: Collaboration Networks
text:
Model
Individuals are represented as nodes, and collaborations are represented as edges. New collaborations form according to the attachment rule
\[
P(i) \propto (k_i + c)^\alpha,
\]
where:

\(k_i\) is the degree of individual \(i\),
\(c\) is the initial-attractiveness parameter, and
\(\alpha\) controls the strength of preferential attachment.

title: A Mathematical Model for Butterfly Wing Patterns
text:
Citation
Traore, E. N. (2017). A Mathematical Model for Butterfly Wing Patterns. Project report supervised by Filippo Remonato and Mats Ehrnstrøm.

title: A Mathematical Model for Butterfly Wing Patterns
text:
Overview
The report studies a mathematical model based on two interacting processes:

A morphogen diffuses across the wing and degrades over time.
The local morphogen concentration activates a gene product that controls later pigmentation.

The author implements the model numerically and investigates how changes in parameters, domain size, and initial morphogen placement affect the resulting wing pattern.

title: A Mathematical Model for Butterfly Wing Patterns
text:
The Model

Morphogen Diffusion
The morphogen concentration \(S\) is governed by
\[
\frac{\partial S}{\partial t}
=
D\nabla^2S
-
K\gamma S.
\]
The equation combines two competing processes:

Diffusion (\(D\nabla^2S\)), which spreads the morphogen across the wing.
Degradation (\(-K\gamma S\)), which removes morphogen over time.

where

\(S\) is the morphogen concentration.
\(\frac{\partial S}{\partial t}\) is the rate of change of \(S\) over time.
\(D\) is the diffusion coefficient.
\(\nabla^2S\) measures how the concentration differs from its surroundings.
\(K\) controls the degradation rate.
\(\gamma\) is a scaling parameter related to wing size.



Gene-Product Activation
The gene product \(g\) satisfies
\[
\frac{\partial g}{\partial t}
=
\gamma
\left(
k_1S
+
\frac{k_2g^2}{1+g^2}
-
k_3g
\right).
\]
The equation combines three competing processes:

Activation by the morphogen (\(k_1S\)), which increases \(g\) when the local morphogen concentration is high.
Nonlinear self-activation \(\left(\frac{k_2g^2}{1+g^2}\right)\), in which existing gene product promotes the production of more gene product.
Degradation (\(-k_3g\)), which removes gene product over time.

where

\(g\) is the concentration of the gene product, the molecule that ultimately influences pigmentation.
\(\frac{\partial g}{\partial t}\) is the rate at which the gene-product concentration changes over time.
\(S\) is the local morphogen concentration.
\(k_1\) controls how strongly the morphogen activates gene production.
\(k_2\) controls the strength of self-activation.
\(k_3\) controls the degradation rate.
\(\gamma\) scales the overall speed of the system.

The nonlinear self-activation term
\[
\frac{k_2g^2}{1+g^2}
\]
has three important properties:

Nonlinear means the rate of activation does not increase at a constant rate as \(g\) increases.
Self-activation means that gene product already present encourages the production of more of itself.
The denominator \(1+g^2\) prevents the activation from increasing indefinitely, causing the term to level off at high concentrations.

Together, self-activation and degradation create a biological switch:

Below a critical morphogen concentration, gene production eventually stops and \(g\) returns to zero.
Above the threshold, the gene product can stabilize at a positive value.
This stable “on” state corresponds to cells that later become pigmented.



Boundary Conditions
The model assumes that morphogen cannot diffuse across

the outer edge of the wing;
wing veins.

This is expressed by the zero-flux boundary condition
\[
\frac{\partial S}{\partial \mathbf{n}}
=
0
\qquad
\text{on } \partial\Omega.
\]
where

\(S\) is the morphogen concentration.
\(\frac{\partial S}{\partial \mathbf{n}}\) is the rate at which the morphogen changes in the direction perpendicular to the boundary.
\(\mathbf{n}\) is the outward normal vector, a vector pointing directly away from the boundary.
\(\partial\Omega\) denotes the boundary of the computational domain.

title: A Mathematical Model for Butterfly Wing Patterns
text:
Numerical Method

Finite Differences

The continuous wing is replaced by a finite grid.
Spatial derivatives are approximated using finite differences.
The Laplacian is computed with a second-order central-difference stencil.



Ghost Nodes

Ghost nodes enforce the zero-flux boundary condition.
Artificial boundary values are chosen so that the normal derivative is zero.
This prevents morphogen from leaving the computational domain.



Time Integration

Time evolution is computed using the forward Euler method.
The emphasis is on reproducing qualitative biological patterns rather than high numerical accuracy.

title: A Mathematical Model for Butterfly Wing Patterns
text:
Main Results

Reproducing Cautery Experiments
The simulations reproduce Murray’s cauterization experiments.

Holes placed near the morphogen source interrupt pigment-band formation.
Holes farther from the source allow pigment bands to develop before diffusion is disrupted.



Effect of Scale
The parameter ()

changes wing size without changing the computational grid;
alters the relative size of the pigmented region.

As () increases, the activated region occupies a smaller portion of the wing.


Constructing a Wing-Shaped Domain
The computational wing is created by

selecting boundary points;
interpolating them with Lagrange polynomials;
embedding the resulting outline in a square computational grid.



Multiple Morphogens
The report also investigates multiple interacting morphogen systems.

Two morphogen fields are simulated simultaneously.
Different gene products produce separate pigment regions.
The approach suggests a pathway toward more complex wing patterns.

title: A Mathematical Model for Butterfly Wing Patterns
text:
Strengths

Converts Murray’s theoretical model into a numerical simulation.
Clearly explains the governing equations.
Clearly explains the boundary conditions.
Clearly explains the numerical implementation.
Uses a wing-shaped computational domain rather than a simple rectangle.
Demonstrates how parameter changes alter biological patterns.
Bridges mathematical theory and computational experimentation.

title: A Mathematical Model for Butterfly Wing Patterns
text:
Limitations

Treats the wing as a largely homogeneous domain.
Does not explicitly model many structural features of real butterfly wings.
Represents geometry indirectly through a finite-difference grid.
A graph-based or irregular-mesh representation may better preserve wing veins and compartment boundaries.

title: A Mathematical Model for Butterfly Wing Patterns
text:
Questions

How sensitive are the simulated patterns to grid resolution?
Would a higher-order or implicit time-stepping method change the results?
Should diffusion coefficients vary across veins or wing compartments?
Could wing boundaries be extracted directly from photographs?
Could the graph Laplacian replace the finite-difference Laplacian?
How should multiple morphogens be coupled?
How can simulated gene-product fields be compared quantitatively with observed pigmentation?
